we got this message from a customer using brain:

Hey team, we keep hitting brain_locked with Brain. Our setup is one Mac with several Claude Code and Codex
agents working in parallel worktrees, all sharing one brain. entire brain brief fails after about 25
seconds. The watch daemon logged 84 lock timeouts in two days, and the processes holding write.lock kept
it for 20 seconds to 1.5 minutes.

Part of it was us. Our prompt hook ran entire brain facts promote --from main on every prompt, and we
changed it to once per session. I could reproduce four more causes on your side (Entire CLI 0.12.2, Brain
0.4.0, macOS arm64):


brief needs the write lock. When another process holds write.lock, brief waits about 25 seconds andthen fails with brain_locked. recall and query work fine at the same time. With --profile-json, 8.5of brief's 15.4 seconds go to status_build_state. Could brief read the last built state instead of takingthe write lock? To reproduce: hold locks/write.lock with flock, then run entire brain brief "x" --json.
facts promote does a full write when there is nothing to copy. It reported promoted: 0 but took 8.75seconds, held write.lock the whole time, and rewrote facts.ndjson and manifest.json. A fast exit whennothing changed would help a lot.
Killing entire does not stop the plugin. If you kill entire brain facts promote (our hook had a4-second timeout), the entire-brain facts promote process keeps running under launchd and keeps the lockuntil it finishes. Passing the signal on to the plugin process would fix that.
The brain is big: 3.9 GB, 540 branch folders, 343,215 facts, and 13.5 million proposal lines. Most branches hold a full copy of main's ~1,000 facts after promote --strategy keep-both. Is that how it is meant to work, and is there a supported way to prune merged branches? I suspect the size makes every write slower, but I have not measured that.


Happy to send the watch log or try a debug build.


----
diagnose what's going on here and how we can fix this

94	//
95	// Under keep-both every conflicting pair is cross-linked (the ADR-P1-G keep-both
96	// guarantee), but the queued proposals are a SPANNING set, not one per pair:
97	// see conflictComponents. Each proposal carries a computed ConflictConfidence
98	// rather than a placeholder, so nothing reaches a human review queue claiming a
99	// confidence this package never derived.
100	func Promote(source, target []Record, strategy, intoBranch string, now time.Time) ([]Record, []Proposal, int) {
101		result := append([]Record(nil), target...)
102		var proposals []Proposal
103		components := newConflictComponents()
104		promoted := 0
105		for _, sf := range source {
106			if sf.Status != StatusActive {
107				continue
108			}
109			sf.Branch = intoBranch
110			if i := IndexOf(result, sf.ID); i >= 0 {
111				result[i].Provenance = UnionAnchors(result[i].Provenance, sf.Provenance)
112				continue
113			}
114			conflicts := activeConflictIndexes(result, sf)
115			if len(conflicts) == 0 {
116				result = append(result, sf)
117				promoted++
118				continue
119			}
120			switch strategy {
121			case "prefer-target":
122				continue // target wins; drop the source fact
123			case "prefer-source":
124				for _, ci := range conflicts {
125					result[ci].Status = StatusSuperseded
126					result[ci].SupersededBy = sf.ID
127					result[ci].UpdatedAt = now
128				}
129				result = append(result, sf)
130				promoted++
131			default: // keep-both
132				for _, ci := range conflicts {
133					result[ci].RelatedIDs = appendUniqueString(result[ci].RelatedIDs, sf.ID)
134					sf.RelatedIDs = appendUniqueString(sf.RelatedIDs, result[ci].ID)
135					// Same-path facts form a clique. A proposal for every pair is
136					// quadratic and tells a reviewer nothing the spanning edges do
137					// not: the review surface groups proposals into connected
138					// components, so one edge into an already-connected component
139					// is pure duplication. Queue only the edges that actually join
140					// two components, which keeps every conflicting fact reachable
141					// in exactly one review group.
142					if components.connected(sf.ID, result[ci].ID) {
143						continue
144					}
145					components.union(sf.ID, result[ci].ID)
146					proposals = append(proposals, Proposal{
147						Action:      ActionSupersede,
148						CandidateID: sf.ID,
149						TargetID:    result[ci].ID,
150						Confidence:  ConflictConfidence(sf, result[ci]),
151						Branch:      intoBranch,
152					})
153				}
154				result = append(result, sf)
155				promoted++
156			}
157		}
158		return result, proposals, promoted
159	}
160	
161	// Retract marks a fact retracted (no longer true) without deleting it, so
162	// the change stays auditable; GC prunes retracted facts later. Returns
163	// whether the fact was found, and whether its status actually changed.
164	func Retract(facts []Record, id string, now time.Time) (found, changed bool) {
165		i := IndexOf(facts, id)
166		if i < 0 {
167			return false, false
168		}
169		if facts[i].Status == StatusRetracted {
170			return true, false
171		}
172		facts[i].Status = StatusRetracted
173		facts[i].UpdatedAt = now
174		return true, true

content.text:
I reproduced the customer's main failure on the current dev build and traced all four causes to specific code. The report checks out.

## Cause 1 — brief needs the write lock: confirmed, but not where they think

`brief` does all its reading without the lock. The failure is at the very end: every retrieval response is emitted through `writeRetrievalResponseBytes` (`internal/cli/retrieval_transport.go:73`), which calls `brainstore.AcquireRetrievalPrivacyPolicies` (`internal/cli/internal/brainstore/retrieval_policy.go:79`). That function acquires the **global brain write lock** before it writes the first byte, to linearize responses against privacy-tombstone writers. The timeout is 10 s per acquisition (`brain_locks.go:17`).

I reproduced it: with `write.lock` held by flock, `brief` fails `brain_locked` after ~12 s and `query` after ~21 s (two acquisitions). `recall` succeeds — it does not pass through this boundary, which also matches the customer's observation. The `--profile-json` output confirms all read stages complete before the failure.

The separate 8.5 s `status_build_state` cost is `factstore.Inspect` (`internal/cli/agent_surface.go:4723`): brief uses the non-lightweight status path, which reads **every branch store** for an integrity check — O(343K facts) on their brain.

**Fix direction:** the emission boundary only needs to exclude tombstone mutations, not promote/distill/remember. Move it to a dedicated tombstone lock (or a shared/reader mode on the lock) so long writers stop blocking every reader's emission. Separately, let brief use the lightweight status path instead of the full integrity scan.

## Cause 2 — no-op promote does a full write: confirmed

`runFactsPromote` (`internal/cli/facts_admin_cmd.go:423`) always calls `factstore.Write` and `updateFactSourceManifestLocked`, even when `promoted == 0`. The manifest refresh is the expensive part (`internal/cli/facts_manifest.go:83`): it runs `factstore.LoadAllBranches` **and** `countFactProposals` over every branch's proposal file, inside the write lock. With 540 branches and 13.5 M proposal lines, that is multi-second per call — and it runs on *every* fact mutation (remember, review, gc, promote). This was already flagged in a recorded review session on 2026-06-10 ("a single `remember` is O(total facts across all branches), entirely inside the exclusive lock") and never fixed.

**Fix direction:** short-circuit promote when `promoted == 0` and no proposals were queued; make the manifest update incremental (touch only the mutated branch's entry).

## Cause 3 — killing `entire` leaves the plugin running: confirmed, with a nuance

I tested both signals on dev:
- SIGTERM to `entire` → the `entire-brain` child dies with it. Forwarding works.
- SIGKILL to `entire` → the child reparents to PID 1 (launchd — that is why their logs say "under launchd") and runs to completion, holding the lock.

Hook runners that enforce timeouts typically escalate to SIGKILL, which no parent can forward. The fix has to be plugin-side: detect parent death (stdin pipe close, or kqueue on the parent pid) and abort. Worth asking the customer which signal their hook sends; if it is SIGTERM, CLI 0.12.2 may simply predate the forwarding that dev already has.

## Cause 4 — branch duplication: by design, and there is no prune

`factmerge.Promote` (`factmerge/admin.go:100`) copies every active source fact into the target branch store — branch stores are deliberately self-contained, so a full copy of main per branch is expected behavior. But there is **no supported way to prune a merged or deleted branch's store**: `memories gc` only prunes retracted/superseded facts within a branch, and the command list has no branch-removal verb. Their suspicion that size slows every write is correct — cause 2 makes every mutation O(all branches + all proposal lines), so 540 dead branch folders directly lengthen every lock hold.

**Fix direction:** add a branch-store prune (e.g. `memories gc --branch <merged-branch> --drop` or a `prune-merged` that checks git for deleted branches). That plus the incremental manifest would shrink their 20 s–1.5 min lock holds dramatically.

## What to tell the customer now

- Their once-per-session promote change was the right call.
- Immediate mitigation: delete dead branch folders' stores manually is not supported today — we should not recommend hand-editing; the prune command is on us.
- Ask which signal their hook sends on timeout, and get the watch log — it will confirm which writers held the lock longest.

Agreed — and it has to be the plugin defending itself, not the dispatcher doing the killing. Two findings from this session shape the design:

**Why the dispatcher can't fully solve it.** I verified on dev that `entire` already forwards SIGTERM — the plugin dies with it. The customer's case is the unforwardable one: a SIGKILL (typical for hook-timeout enforcement) gives the parent no chance to forward anything, and macOS has no `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG` equivalent. After the parent dies, the plugin reparents to PID 1 and runs to completion holding `write.lock`. So the only reliable fix is orphan detection inside `entire-brain`.

**The design I'd propose:**

- At startup, record `os.Getppid()`. If it is already 1, don't arm (that's the launchd watch daemon — legitimate).
- A watchdog goroutine polls `os.Getppid()` about once per second. When it no longer matches the original ppid, the parent is gone: print one line to stderr and `os.Exit(1)`.
- Immediate exit is safe here, no graceful teardown needed: every store write goes through `WriteBrainRelativeFileAtomic` (atomic rename) and flock releases on process exit. An aborted promote loses its batch but cannot corrupt the store — and freeing the lock fast is the whole point.
- Compare against the *original* ppid rather than checking `== 1`, so it also behaves correctly under subreapers (Linux containers).

**One trap to avoid:** the setup backfill is spawned detached with `Setsid: true` (`internal/cli/setup_spawn.go:37`) and is *supposed* to outlive its spawner. A naive "ppid changed → die" watchdog would kill it. The clean discriminator: a `Setsid` child is a session leader (`Getsid(0) == Getpid()`), a dispatched plugin is not. Arm the watchdog only for non-session-leaders. That exempts the backfill automatically, with no env-var plumbing.

Polling at 1 s is deliberately lazy but sufficient — the lock holds we're fixing run 8–90 s, so worst case adds one second. kqueue `NOTE_EXIT` would be instant but needs per-platform code for a latency win nobody will notice.

Alternatives I'd reject: watching stdin for EOF (depends on how the dispatcher wires stdin, and some commands read stdin for data, e.g. `facts import`); fixing only the dispatcher (doesn't help SIGKILL, and doesn't protect customers on older `entire` versions).

# Handoff: entire-brain must exit when its dispatcher dies (event-driven, no polling)

## Problem

A customer runs many agents in parallel against one shared brain. Their prompt
hook killed `entire brain facts promote` after a 4-second timeout, but the
`entire-brain` plugin child kept running and held `locks/write.lock` until it
finished (20 s to 1.5 min). Every concurrent reader then failed `brain_locked`.

Verified on dev (2026-11-01, macOS arm64):

- SIGTERM to `entire` is forwarded; the plugin exits with it. Already covered.
- SIGKILL to `entire` cannot be forwarded. The plugin reparents to PID 1 and
  runs to completion, holding the write lock. This is the gap. Hook runners
  commonly escalate to SIGKILL on timeout.

Reproduction:

```
entire brain brief "signal kill test" --json & PARENT=$!
sleep 0.7
CHILD=$(pgrep -P $PARENT | head -1)
kill -KILL $PARENT
ps -o pid,ppid,stat,command -p $CHILD   # child alive, PPID now 1
```

## Requirement

Plugin-side orphan detection that blocks on an OS event. Do NOT use a
`Getppid()` polling loop on a timer — that approach was proposed and
explicitly rejected.

## Design

Add a small package (suggested: `internal/cli/internal/parentwatch`) with one
entry point, `Arm()`, called from `cli.Execute` (`internal/cli/root.go:46`).
`Arm()` records the original ppid, registers the platform watcher, and starts
one goroutine that blocks until the parent exits, then writes one line to
stderr ("parent process exited; aborting") and calls `os.Exit(1)`.

Platform watchers (all are blocking waits, no timers):

- darwin/BSD: kqueue `EVFILT_PROC` with `NOTE_EXIT` on the original ppid
  (`golang.org/x/sys/unix`: `Kqueue` + one blocking `Kevent`).
- linux: `unix.PidfdOpen(ppid, 0)`, then block in `unix.Poll` on the pidfd;
  it becomes readable when the parent exits (kernel >= 5.3). If `PidfdOpen`
  returns `ENOSYS`, fall back to `prctl(PR_SET_PDEATHSIG, SIGTERM)` set from
  the child, then re-check `Getppid()` once. Document the PDEATHSIG caveat
  (it tracks the parent thread, not strictly the process).
- windows: `OpenProcess(SYNCHRONIZE, false, ppid)` +
  `WaitForSingleObject(handle, INFINITE)`.

Registration race: after registering the watcher, re-check `os.Getppid()`
once. If it no longer matches the recorded original, the parent died before
registration — exit immediately.

## Arming rules (critical — getting these wrong kills legitimate daemons)

1. Do not arm when the initial `Getppid()` is 1. The launchd watch daemon
   starts with ppid 1 and must keep running.
2. Do not arm for intentionally detached children. `spawnDetached`
   (`internal/cli/setup_spawn.go:25`) launches the backfill with
   `Setsid: true` and it must outlive its spawner. Make the exemption
   explicit: set an env var (e.g. `ENTIRE_BRAIN_DETACHED=1`) in the detached
   spawn's env and skip arming when it is present. A unix session-leader
   check (`unix.Getsid(0) == os.Getpid()`) is a reasonable extra guard, but
   the env var is the portable contract and covers Windows.
3. Everything dispatched by the `entire` CLI should arm. That is the default.

## Safety of immediate exit

`os.Exit(1)` on parent death is safe. All store writes go through
`WriteBrainRelativeFileAtomic` (atomic rename), and flock releases on process
exit. An aborted mutation loses only its batch; it cannot corrupt the store.
Releasing `write.lock` fast is the whole point.

## Acceptance

- Unit tests for the arming rules with an injectable ppid/env source.
- One integration check: a test parent execs a helper that arms parentwatch,
  SIGKILL the parent, assert the child exits promptly (event-driven, so
  well under a second) and that a held flock is released. Skip cleanly on
  platforms where the harness cannot run it.
- `gofmt -l -s` and `go vet` clean (this repo's CI gate; there is no oxfmt
  binary here).
- Run `go test` directly on the touched packages. Do not use
  `mise run check` / `test:integration` — they fail locally for a missing
  gotestsum, not for real failures.

## Out of scope

- Dispatcher-side changes (the `entire` CLI repo). Linux `Pdeathsig` on the
  plugin spawn would be defense in depth, but it is another repo and another
  task.
- The other three brain_locked causes (retrieval emission takes the global
  write lock; no-op `facts promote` rewrites the store and rebuilds the
  manifest O(all branches + all proposals); no prune for dead branch stores).
  Those are being handled in the tegucigalpa workspace.

## Background evidence

Brain memory `fact:1d10ce176f39425716a28b6e` (branch
`evisdren/brain_locked-write.lock-fix`) records the full four-cause customer
diagnosis. Retrieve with:

```
entire brain recall "brain_locked customer diagnosis" --branch evisdren/brain_locked-write.lock-fix --json
```

# Handoff: `facts promote` no-op fast exit + incremental manifest update

## Problem

A customer ran `entire brain facts promote --from main` from a prompt hook on
every prompt, across many parallel agents sharing one brain (3.9 GB, 540
branch folders, 343,215 facts, 13.5 M proposal lines). A promote that copied
nothing (`promoted: 0`) still:

- held `locks/write.lock` for 8.75 s,
- rewrote the target branch's `facts.ndjson`,
- rewrote `manifest.json` (and the README).

These lock holds are a major source of the `brain_locked` failures other
readers and writers hit. This was already flagged in a recorded review on
2026-06-10 ("a single `remember` is O(total facts across all branches),
entirely inside the exclusive lock") and never fixed.

## Where the cost is

`runFactsPromote` (`internal/cli/facts_admin_cmd.go:423`):

1. Under `WithBrainWriteLock`: loads source and target branch stores, merges
   via `factmerge.Promote`, then **unconditionally** `factstore.Write`s the
   target (line 438) and calls `updateFactSourceManifestLocked` (line 447).
2. `updateFactSourceManifestLocked` (`internal/cli/facts_manifest.go:83`) is
   the dominant cost: `factstore.LoadAllBranches` parses **every** branch
   store, and `countFactProposals` parses **every** branch's proposals file
   (the 13.5 M lines), all inside the write lock, to recompute totals that a
   single-branch mutation could compute as a delta.

## Scope: two fixes, both in this task

### 1. No-op fast exit

When the merge changed nothing, skip the store write and the manifest update
entirely and release the lock immediately.

Careful with "changed nothing": `promoted == 0 && len(proposals) == 0` is NOT
sufficient. `factmerge.Promote` (`factmerge/admin.go:100`) unions provenance
onto existing identical-ID facts (lines 110-112), which mutates the target
even when nothing is counted as promoted. The clean fix is to make the change
detectable at the source: have `factmerge.Promote` report whether it mutated
the target (a changed count or bool — e.g. count provenance unions), rather
than deep-comparing slices after the fact. `factmerge` is a pure package;
keep it that way.

Output contract: `promoted: 0` summaries must look exactly as they do today
(JSON keys and text line unchanged); this is a performance change, not a
behavior change.

### 2. Incremental manifest update for single-branch mutations

Add a variant of the manifest update for the common case "one branch's store
changed, and the caller holds both the before and after fact slices":

```
updateFactSourceManifestForBranchLocked(brainDir, branch string, before, after []factRecord, proposalDelta int, now time.Time) error
```

- Load the existing manifest, adjust `Sources.Facts` totals (facts,
  distilled, authored, imported, superseded, by_kind, proposals) by the
  delta between `before` and `after` for that one branch, keep the
  `Branches` list correct (a branch that gains its first store gets added).
- Preserve everything `preserveFactDistillEvidence`
  (`internal/cli/facts_manifest.go:114`) preserves today — the incremental
  path must not blank distill evidence fields.
- If the manifest has no facts source yet, or anything about the stored
  state makes the delta unsafe to apply (e.g. the manifest declares counts

Both tombstone writers (`session_privacy.go:448` include flow, `session_privacy.go:1604` exclude/purge via `executeSessionCleanup`) run inside the existing write-lock critical sections, and `runPrivacyLinearizedPatternMutation` (`pattern_privacy.go:22`) piggybacks on the emission boundary to get write protection for pattern mutations — that's the one subtle dependency.

**Handoff for the no-op promote is ready at `.context/handoff-noop-promote-manifest.md`** (absolute: `/Users/evisdrenova/conductor/workspaces/entire-brain/tegucigalpa/.context/handoff-noop-promote-manifest.md`). It covers both the quick win and the fundamental fix:
- No-op fast exit — with the trap called out that `promoted == 0` is not enough, because `factmerge.Promote` unions provenance onto identical facts; the change signal has to come from `Promote` itself.
- Incremental manifest update — a delta-based `updateFactSourceManifestForBranchLocked` replacing the O(all branches + all 13.5 M proposal lines) rebuild, with fallback to the full recompute whenever the delta is unsafe, plus a consistency test (incremental result must equal full recompute).

**Emission lock — proposed design for your sign-off before I implement:**

The recorded decisions don't require the emission boundary to use the global write lock; it was used because tombstone writers already held it. The invariant that must survive: no tombstone or derived-state change may linearize between the final privacy re-check and the last response byte.

1. New lock `locks/retrieval-policy.lock`, with a **shared/exclusive** flock mode added to `AcquireFileLock` (LOCK_SH on unix, non-exclusive LockFileEx on Windows).
2. **Response emission** (`AcquireRetrievalPrivacyPolicies`, retrieval_policy.go:79) takes the policy lock **shared** instead of write.lock. Concurrent briefs stop serializing each other, and promote/distill/remember writers stop blocking emissions entirely.
3. **Privacy mutators** (the two tombstone flows and the cleanup/rebuild they drive) additionally take the policy lock **exclusive**, inside their existing write-lock span. Ordering rule: `privacy-side-effect.lock → write.lock → retrieval-policy.lock`; emission takes only the policy lock, so no cycle is possible.
4. `runPrivacyLinearizedPatternMutation` currently gets write protection for free from the boundary — it must now take write.lock itself plus the policy lock exclusive, same ordering.
5. The existing race-seam tests (`beforeRetrievalResponseWrite` etc.) get updated to prove the invariant against the new lock; my flock repro from the diagnosis becomes an integration test: hold write.lock, brief must now succeed.

One accepted risk to state: during a binary upgrade, an old process's tombstone write (write.lock only) could race a new process's emission (policy lock only) in the narrow recheck-to-write window. Privacy excludes are rare, human-initiated operations, and the overlap window is transient; I'd document it rather than version-gate.

Separately, brief's 8.5 s `status_build_state` (the full `factstore.Inspect` integrity scan) is untouched by this — worth a small follow-up to use the lightweight status path, but it's a different change.

walk me through this emission and lock issue in simple straightforward technial language. be very concise

**The setup.** A brain can "tombstone" a session — mark it private. Nothing tombstoned may ever appear in command output. So `brief`/`query`/`get` work in two steps: build the whole response in memory, then do a final privacy check and write the bytes.

**The invariant.** Between that final check and the last byte written, no tombstone may land. Otherwise you could emit content that was just marked private.

**How it's enforced today.** Tombstone writers hold the brain's global `write.lock`. So the emitter grabs the same `write.lock` around check-and-write (`retrieval_policy.go:79`). That's correct, but too broad: *every* writer uses that lock — `promote`, distill, `remember`. A 30-second promote blocks every brief's final write, which times out after 10 s with `brain_locked`. That's the customer's failure.

**The fix.** The emitter only needs to exclude *tombstone* changes, not all writes. So: add a dedicated `retrieval-policy.lock`.

- Emitters take it **shared** — they don't block each other, and don't touch `write.lock` at all.
- Tombstone writers take it **exclusive** (in addition to `write.lock` they already hold).

Result: brief vs. promote — no conflict. Brief vs. tombstone write — still mutually excluded, invariant intact.

**Two details.** Fixed lock order (`write.lock` before `retrieval-policy.lock`) prevents deadlock; emitters only take the one lock. And one code path (`runPrivacyLinearizedPatternMutation`) currently uses the emission boundary to get write protection for free — it must start taking `write.lock` itself.
if we remove the tombstone and the ability to mark it as private, is this still an issue?

Yes — the emission lock exists *only* to enforce the tombstone invariant. Remove tombstones and the whole final-boundary lock (`AcquireRetrievalPrivacyPolicies`, the buffering, the re-check) can be deleted, not just narrowed. The brief/query `brain_locked`-at-emission failure disappears.

Two caveats:

1. **It doesn't remove all read-side blocking.** A brief with a stale history FTS index still takes `write.lock` to rebuild it (`history_fts.go:142`). That's rarer (only when stale) and it's a real write. And writer-vs-writer contention — promote, distill, remember fighting each other — is untouched; that's the no-op-promote/manifest work, which matters regardless.

2. **The feature is load-bearing.** Tombstone + purge is the only way to make a session unreadable after the fact — the recorded decision (fact:991cb0f3) moved enforcement to the read path precisely because file deletion can't enforce a purge once derived copies exist. Brains hold full transcripts; people paste credentials and PII into agent sessions. Dropping exclude/purge means an accidentally captured secret is permanently retrievable (and syncs to hosted, where connected). That's a product and compliance regression, not just a code simplification.

So: technically yes, it kills this issue at the root. But I wouldn't trade the purge capability for it when the dedicated-lock fix keeps both — the lock split is a contained change, and the invariant machinery (buffering, identity re-check) all stays as-is around a different lock.

If the real question is "is the privacy feature worth its complexity" — that's a product call worth raising explicitly, not a side effect to reach through a lock fix.

Good instinct — I pulled the introduction commit, and the answer is: **not leftover, but an explicit stopgap.**

Session exclusion/tombstones landed 2026-08-07 (`4b5cdfd3`), fully aware of the checkpoint architecture. The commit says it directly:

> "The canonical capture on entire/checkpoints/v1 is the capture layer's data and is deliberately untouched (the plan's resolved brain-local-tombstone default **until a capture-layer exclusion contract exists**)."

The threat it covers is the one you identified yourself: redaction at checkpoint capture is pattern-based, so something sensitive can survive it into a checkpoint. From there the brain copies it into several places of its own — transcript copies under `sessions/`, the FTS index, the scan cache, the conversation store, and potentially distilled facts (which sync hosted). The feature's canary test plants a secret in one session and proves purge removes it from every brain-local store. Upstream redaction can't help once the content is already in a checkpoint; this is the only pull-it-back-out mechanism.

Two details worth knowing before retiring it:

- Tombstones survive re-export: a purged session that the capture layer exports again stays un-indexed. Without tombstones, "delete the checkpoint upstream + `brain refresh`" only works if upstream reliably stops exporting that session.
- Facts distilled from a bad session are brain-created artifacts; no capture-layer contract covers them. Purge filters those too.

So the real question is the one the commit left open: **does a capture-layer exclusion contract exist now?** If yes, retiring brain-local tombstones is coherent — and then the emission boundary (buffering, identity re-check, the lock) gets deleted outright rather than re-locked, which is strictly simpler.

My suggestion: don't couple that product decision to the `brain_locked` fix. The lock split is small and doesn't change any contract; retiring the privacy layer is a bigger call you can make separately — and if you do, the lock split code mostly deletes along with it. Want me to proceed with the lock split, or hold while you decide on the tombstone question?

You're right, and I had the architecture partially wrong. I verified the pipeline in the code. Here is what actually exists:

**Verified infrastructure:**
- The brain reads checkpoints **directly from git refs** — `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` and the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch, via a `git cat-file --batch` child (`export.go:50-54`, `runner.go:37`). There is no separate capture store. Export even refuses to run without local checkpoint refs: *"persistent transcript storage requires local checkpoint refs; sync checkpoints and retry"* (`export.go:349`).
- The brain's `sessions/` directory is a **derived transcript cache** of those git bytes, swept on every refresh (`sweepTranscriptCache`). It is not an independent transcript store.
- One deliberate exception: when a checkpoint's bytes vanish from git (e.g. a deleted feature branch destroyed a commit-style checkpoint), the sweep *retains* the cached transcript as "the only surviving copy" (`export.go:410-415`) — the cache can outlive git there.

**What this changes in my assessment:** my earlier privacy framing was overstated. A checkpoint lives in a shared git branch, pushed to origin — anyone with repo access can read it. So a brain-local purge never deletes anything; it only stops *this brain* from indexing and serving it. The tombstone is suppression, not deletion. The real deletion primitive in this architecture belongs at the git layer: remove the checkpoint from the shared branch, and brains rebuild from git — which is exactly the "capture-layer exclusion contract" the Aug 7 commit said it was waiting for.

**So the decision is now clean:**

- **Option A — keep brain-local tombstones:** then the emission boundary stays and the lock split is the right contained fix.
- **Option B — deletion moves to the git layer** (fits the architecture you're describing): the entire privacy read gate, response buffering, identity re-check, and the emission lock get **deleted**, not re-locked. The `brain_locked`-at-emission failure disappears structurally. That path needs two accompanying changes: make the sweep mirror git strictly (drop or gate the retain-last-copy behavior), and filter/re-distill facts by session provenance on rebuild so a deleted session's influence leaves the fact store too.

Option B is the fundamental fix and the simpler end state; it is also a bigger change (the whole `privacy` command family, gates, canary tests) and it depends on the git-layer deletion contract actually existing in the capture side of the CLI. Causes 2–4 (promote cost, signals, pruning) are unaffected either way.

Which direction do you want? If B, I'd start by scoping the removal and verifying what the capture layer offers today for checkpoint deletion — and I'll record the verified architecture in Brain either way so this doesn't get re-litigated from the old mental model.

content.text:
Good news: most of it already exists. `entire checkpoint delete` removes a checkpoint locally and from every checkpoint remote, and on the v1 aggregate branch it removes it from the **branch tip** (history still contains it). The brain reads only checkpoint ref tips, so tip-removal is exactly the visibility cut the brain would honor on its next refresh.

"The git-layer deletion contract" is the set of guarantees that command family must make so the brain can carry **zero privacy state of its own**. Concretely, four pieces:

1. **Session-level completeness** *(gap, cli repo)*. Today's delete is per-checkpoint and explicitly leaves sibling checkpoints of the same session ("the session stays visible while any of them remain"). The contract needs "delete session" semantics — all checkpoints carrying that transcript, in one operation.

2. **Anti-resurrection** *(the critical gap, cli repo)*. This is what tombstones currently provide ("a purged session that the capture layer re-exports stays un-indexed"). With multiple clones, a machine that hasn't fetched yet still has the checkpoint on its local v1 branch — when it pushes, does the deletion survive the merge, or does the checkpoint come back? The contract needs a deletion record that lives **on the v1 branch itself**, so it propagates and merges like all other checkpoint data. Whether the CLI already has this is the main thing to verify in the cli repo; the help's "re-enabling push_sessions later pushes the removal" hints the sync layer treats removal as state, but that's not confirmation.

3. **Honest deletion tier** *(policy statement)*. Tip-removal leaves bytes in branch history and unreferenced objects until GC. That's the same exposure today's tombstone leaves, so it's not a regression — but the contract should say it plainly: this is "stop indexing and serving everywhere," not cryptographic erasure.

4. **Brain mirrors git, strictly** *(this repo)*. Refresh drops everything not reachable from current checkpoint tips: remove the retain-last-copy sweep behavior (`export.go:410-415`), filter facts by session provenance on rebuild (facts carry `session_id` provenance, so this is mechanical), and delete the privacy layer — tombstone store, read gates, response buffering, identity re-check, emission lock, the `privacy` command family.

One semantics change to accept: deletion takes effect at the next refresh, not mid-response. "Stop serving now" becomes `entire checkpoint delete … && entire brain refresh`. The per-response linearization machinery exists only to make tombstones instantaneous; Option B trades that instant cutover for no response-time locking at all.

Suggested next step: I verify point 2 against the cli repo (is there a deletion record on the v1 branch, or does a stale clone's push resurrect?) — that answer decides whether Option B is implementable now or needs a cli-side change first. Want me to dig into that?
what are we actually deleting though?

Concretely, three buckets:

**1. The thing being deleted: the session transcript.** A checkpoint carries the session's **full transcript** (the delete help says so directly) — prompts, agent responses, tool calls and their output — tied to a commit, post-redaction, stored as files on the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch tip. That transcript is the sensitive object. Redaction is pattern-based, so what slips through is whatever doesn't look like a known secret: pasted customer data, a prod connection string in an odd format, code from a repo that shouldn't leak, an HR conversation someone had in the wrong terminal. `checkpoint delete` removes it from the v1 tip, locally, on checkpoint remotes, and (per the help) it's what makes the session stop being visible on entire.com.

**2. What the brain drops as a consequence (derivatives of that transcript).** This is what today's purge plan enumerates and what a strict-mirror refresh would rebuild without: the cached transcript copy under `sessions/`, its history-index records and excerpts, the FTS rows, the scan cache, conversation-store exchanges, episodes/pattern-corpus entries built from it, and **facts distilled from it** (filterable by `session_id` provenance). None of this is independent data — it's all recomputable projections of the checkpoint.

**3. What is *not* deleted — the honest residue.**
- Bytes in v1 branch **history** and unreachable git objects, until GC on each clone/remote.
- Copies on **other machines' clones** until they fetch (and the resurrection question from before).
- **Hosted facts already synced**: a fact distilled from the deleted session may have gone out over the per-fact wire. Local rebuild drops it; whether hosted reconciles that removal is an open question to verify — otherwise the fact outlives its source.

So the operation is precisely: "this conversation should stop existing as a retrievable record, everywhere downstream" — transcript at the source, projections by rebuild. If nobody ever needs that operation, the whole contract is moot and the privacy layer deletes even more cheaply. But that's the question in reverse: you don't need tombstones *or* the contract until the day someone pastes the wrong thing into an agent session, and then you need one of them to exist.

Yes — stated that way, the model is simple and the code should match it:

**Checkpoints are the source of truth; deletion originates in the entire CLI (`entire checkpoint delete`); the brain is a derived index that mirrors whatever the checkpoint refs currently say.** Refresh sees a checkpoint gone → every derivative of it goes too: cached transcript, index records, FTS rows, conversation exchanges, episodes, and distilled facts (by `session_id` provenance). No brain-side deletion API, no tombstones, no privacy state. Propagation and resurrection-prevention across clones are checkpoint-sync concerns in the CLI — if a stale clone pushes a deleted checkpoint back, the brain faithfully re-indexes it, and the fix belongs in the sync, not in brain state.

What that deletes from this repo:

- The tombstone store and the whole `privacy` command family (exclude/include/purge/list).
- The read gates (`requirePrivacyDerivedRead`, derived-dirty gate) and the response machinery — buffering, identity re-check, and the emission lock. **Cause 1 dies structurally: nothing is acquired at emission time.**
- The retain-last-copy sweep behavior (`export.go:410-415`) — the one spot where the brain deliberately outlives git, which contradicts the mirror model.

Two real decisions hiding in "delete those as well", worth settling up front:

1. **Facts with mixed provenance.** A distilled fact can cite several sessions. Rule I'd propose: drop the deleted session's provenance entries; drop the fact only when a distilled fact has no provenance left. Authored facts (`remember`) have no session anchor and are untouched — they're the brain's own memories, which fits your framing.
2. **Hosted facts.** A dropped fact may already have synced over the per-fact wire. The removal has to propagate (likely as a retract/supersede over the same wire) or hosted keeps a fact whose source is gone. Needs verification against the frozen sync surface during implementation.

And one semantics note: deletion converges at the next refresh — the watch daemon ticks anyway, so in practice it's automatic, just not mid-response-instant like tombstones were. That's the trade, and I think it's the right one.

## Why

Response emission (brief, query, get, workspace, handoff, dash, viz) acquired the global brain write lock around the final privacy check and the output write. Any long-running writer — promote, distill flush, remember — failed every concurrent reader with `brain_locked` after the 10 s lock timeout. A customer running parallel agents against one shared brain hit this constantly (reported: `brief` failing after ~25 s whenever any agent was writing; 84 lock timeouts in two days).

## What changed

- Emission now revalidates the captured privacy-policy identity and derived-read gate **without locks** (`brainstore.ValidateRetrievalPrivacyPolicies`), then writes. A policy change before the check still fails the response closed.
- The instant-suppression guarantee is deliberately retired: a tombstone landing between the final check and the output write takes effect on the next command instead of invalidating the in-flight response. This is step 1 of retiring brain-local privacy state in favor of checkpoint-level deletion mirrored by refresh.
- `WithLockedRetrievalPrivacyPolicies` remains for the pattern/corpus mutation paths (`runPrivacyLinearizedPatternMutation`, `BuildWorkspaceCorpus`), which use the member-brain locks for mutual exclusion.
- Deleted the three tests that proved the retired linearization; added two that pin the new contract (emission succeeds while another process holds the write lock; emission does not hold the lock during the output write). Dead `acquireRetrievalPrivacyPolicies` removed.

## Validation

- Full `go test ./internal/cli` green (273 s); brainstore and patterns packages green; `gofmt -l -s` and `go vet ./...` clean.
- All late-tombstone fail-closed tests pass unchanged.
- End-to-end on a real 24k-fact brain: with `locks/write.lock` held by another process, `brief` succeeds in 6 s and `query` succeeds — both previously failed `brain_locked`.

## Known residual

A stale derived index (doc/history FTS) still waits one 10 s write-lock timeout on the read path under writer contention, then degrades to a lock-free fallback and succeeds. That path goes away with the no-caches/stateless-brain direction, not this PR.

What shipped (+91/−256, net deletion):

- Emission revalidates the privacy policy **without locks** (`ValidateRetrievalPrivacyPolicies`) and writes; a policy change before the check still fails closed. The instant-suppression guarantee is retired — a tombstone landing mid-write takes effect on the next command. The locked variant survives only for the pattern/corpus mutation paths until the privacy layer is removed wholesale.
- Tests: the three linearization tests proving the retired guarantee are deleted; two new ones pin the new contract (emission succeeds while another process holds `write.lock`; emission never holds the lock during output). All fail-closed late-tombstone tests pass unchanged.

# Review PR

Review a pull request with structured, actionable feedback.

## Arguments

- `` — PR number, URL, or branch name. If empty, review the current branch's open PR.

## Process

### 1. Fetch PR context

```

```

Read the PR description carefully — it defines scope and intent. Everything you review should be evaluated against what the PR is trying to accomplish.

### 2. Understand the change

Before reviewing line-by-line:
- What is this PR doing and why?
- What files are touched and what's the blast radius?
- Are there any architectural implications?

### 3. Review with this checklist

**Correctness**
- Does the code do what the PR description says?
- Are there logic errors, off-by-one bugs, or unhandled edge cases?
- Are error paths handled correctly?

**Security**
- Any injection risks (SQL, XSS, command injection)?
- Are secrets, tokens, or credentials handled safely?
- Are inputs validated at system boundaries?

**Testing**
- Are there tests for the new/changed behavior?
- Do tests cover edge cases, not just the happy path?
- Are test assertions meaningful (not just "doesn't throw")?

**Design**
- Does the change follow existing codebase patterns and conventions?
- Is the abstraction level appropriate (not over/under-engineered)?
- Are there unnecessary changes outside the stated scope?

**Performance**
- Any N+1 queries, unbounded loops, or missing pagination?
- Are there opportunities for batching or caching that were missed?
- Will this scale with the data sizes it will encounter?

**Readability**
- Are names clear and consistent with the codebase?
- Is complex logic adequately explained?
- Would a future reader understand the "why" behind non-obvious decisions?

### 4. Adversarial review

Take a second, adversarial pass over the diff. Actively try to break the change — assume it has flaws and hunt for them across:

- **Performance** — worst-case inputs, hot paths, allocations, contention.
- **Stability** — race conditions, partial failures, retries, resource leaks, crash recovery.
- **Correctness** — inputs and states that violate the author's assumptions.
- **Simplicity** — code that could be deleted or replaced with something simpler/stdlib.
- **Platform design standards** — deviations from the platform's established design patterns and conventions.

Add any findings to the output using the same severity format.

### 5. Run /simplify

Run the `/simplify` skill (via the Skill tool) against the changed code and fold its findings into the review output.

### 6. Structure your output

For each finding, use this format:

**[severity] file:line — short title**
Description of the issue and why it matters. Include a suggested fix when possible.

Severity levels:
- **[blocking]** — Must fix before merge. Correctness bugs, security issues, data loss risks.
- **[important]** — Should fix. Design problems, missing tests for critical paths, performance issues.
- **[nit]** — Nice to fix. Style, naming, minor improvements. Don't block merge on these.
- **[question]** — Not necessarily wrong, but needs clarification or discussion.

### 7. Summary

End with a brief summary:
- Overall assessment (approve / request changes / needs discussion)
- What the PR does well
- Top 1-3 items that need attention
- Any scope concerns (changes that seem unrelated to the stated goal)

## Guidelines

- Review what's in the diff, not what you wish was there. Don't request unrelated refactoring.
- If the PR is large, focus on the most impactful files first.
- Be specific — "this could be better" is not useful. Show what "better" looks like.
- Distinguish between "this is wrong" and "I would do this differently." Only the former is blocking.
- If you're unsure about something, use [question] severity instead of asserting it's wrong.
- Read relevant source files (not just the diff) when you need context about how changed code integrates with the rest of the system.

content.text:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

content.text:
Review complete, fixes applied and pushed (`aadbdd2f`), full suite green, PR body updated. The review report:

## Findings

**[important] internal/cli/recall_evidence.go:59 — pure read still took every brain write lock** *(fixed)*
`recall --evidence` ran through `runPrivacyLinearizedPatternMutation`, which acquires the brain write locks — despite its own comment saying the path "never invokes a provider or writes derived facts". It still failed `brain_locked` under any concurrent writer, i.e. the exact defect this PR exists to fix, on a surface the PR missed. Moved to `bufferRetrievalCommandOutput` with emission-time revalidation; its lock test now asserts the inverse contract.

**[important] internal/cli/retrieval_transport.go:79 — dead `transactional` branch bypassed validation** *(fixed)*
No type anywhere implements `writeRetrievalResponse([]byte, []retrievalPrivacyPolicy)` (this predates the PR), and any future implementor would have skipped `ValidateRetrievalPrivacyPolicies` entirely. Deleted.

**[nit] brainstore/retrieval_policy.go — identity/derived-clean check loop duplicated** *(fixed)*
`ValidateRetrievalPrivacyPolicies` and `AcquireRetrievalPrivacyPolicies` carried identical loops that could drift. Both now call `validateNormalizedRetrievalPolicies`.

**[nit] retrieval_transport.go — orphaned seam, duplicated sequence, stale name** *(fixed)*
`beforeRetrievalResponseWrite` had no remaining users (deleted); the validate-then-write sequence existed twice (`commitRetrievalResponse` now shared); `privacyLinearizedWriter` renamed `privacyCheckedWriter`.

**[nit] stale comments claiming emission holds the write lock** *(fixed)*
`pattern_corpus.go:198`, `viz/viz.go:250`, `viz/deps.go:32`, `retrieve/deps.go:56`.

**[question → deferred] workspace_patterns.go — `workspace patterns list` rebuilds the corpus under member-brain locks.** A real write inside a list command; needs its own design and fits the privacy-layer-removal follow-up. Noted in the PR body.

**Skipped deliberately:** reusing `writeAllCommandBytes` for the short-write check (it skips empty writes and rewraps errors — different semantics tests depend on); caching the dashboard's per-draw guard load (pre-existing cost, out of scope).

## Summary

**Approve** (as author post-fix: ready for a human pass). The core design held up under all four review angles — the unlocked validation does strictly less I/O than the old locked path, the race detector is clean, and every fail-closed late-tombstone test passes unchanged. The one real catch was `recall --evidence`: the PR originally chose lock behavior by *which wrapper a command used* rather than by *whether it mutates*, and that stranded one reader on the old failure mode. Worth keeping in mind for the privacy-layer removal: classify paths by mutation, not by plumbing.

content.text:
**What it is.** `entire brain memories promote` (older alias: `facts promote`) copies one branch's active memories into another branch's store: `promote --from main` or `promote --from <feature> --into main`. Flags: `--from` (required), `--into` (defaults to the current branch), `--strategy keep-both|prefer-source|prefer-target`.

**Where it lives.** Command and orchestration in `internal/cli/facts_admin_cmd.go:342` (`runFactsPromote` at `:423`); the pure merge logic in the exported `factmerge` package (`factmerge/admin.go:100`). Added 2026-06-05 (`fa8dad3c`) together with `facts review` and `facts gc`.

**Why it exists.** Memories are branch-scoped: a fact distilled from a session on branch X goes into X's store only, so unmerged work can't pollute main's memory, and recall answers from the branch you're on. The cost of that isolation is that memory does not follow git — merging a feature branch merges its code but not its memories, and deleting the branch would strand them. Promote is the explicit, manual carry across that gap, in both directions:

- *upstream*: after merging a feature branch, `promote --from <feature> --into main` so its decisions survive (it deliberately works for already-deleted branches whose stores remain);
- *downstream*: seed a fresh feature branch with main's memories — which is exactly what the customer's per-prompt hook was doing.

Merge semantics: identical facts (same content-derived ID) merge their provenance; same-path conflicts follow the strategy, where `keep-both` keeps both facts, cross-links them, and queues supersede proposals for human review.

**Recorded history worth knowing:**
- A closed-negative on main says it outright: *"keep-both results in an unmanageable volume of conflict proposals on dense branches; use prefer-\* strategies"* — which is the customer's 13.5 M proposal lines, predicted.
- Earlier sync versions (v1/v2) had automatic promote-on-merge; it was rejected for v3 because branch-keyed heads broke teammate distribution of merged facts. So the manual command is what survived of that idea.

One forward-looking note: in your stateless target, promote is a symptom of memories being a branch-keyed side store. If memories derive from checkpoints, "what does a branch know" could follow git topology (a branch sees its ancestors' facts) instead of physical copies — that would delete promote, the duplication, and the pruning problem in one move. Worth keeping on the table when we get past the lock work.

okay before i merge this: walk em through it very concisely. what is the core problem, how do we solve it and why this solve work. simple, straightforward technical language.

**The problem.** Every brain command that prints results — `brief`, `query`, `get` — grabbed the global `write.lock` right before printing. The lock existed to guarantee that a session marked private mid-command could never appear in output. But it's the same lock every writer uses, so a 30-second `promote` or distill made every concurrent reader wait 10 s and die with `brain_locked`. Readers were paying a writer's price for a guarantee about one rare event (marking a session private).

**The solve.** Build the response, then do a lock-free final check before printing: reload the privacy state, compare it to the state the response was built under. Match → print. Changed → fail closed, no bytes out. No lock acquired, ever, on the read path.

**Why it works.**

1. *Safety is preserved where it matters.* A response built from now-private data still never escapes: the final check sees the changed state and kills it. All the existing fail-closed tests pass unchanged.
2. *What we gave up is tiny and deliberate.* If the privacy mark lands in the microseconds between the check and the bytes hitting stdout, that one response still goes out; the mark takes effect on the next command. That instant-cutover was the only thing the lock bought — and since we're removing brain-local privacy marks entirely (deletion moves to the checkpoint layer), we're paying nothing for a guarantee that's about to not exist.
3. *Readers and writers no longer share anything.* A promote can hold the lock for a minute; briefs don't care. Two briefs don't even serialize against each other anymore.

# Handoff: remove the brain-local privacy layer (tombstones, gates, privacy commands)

## Decision context (already made — do not re-litigate)

The brain is a derived index over git-resident checkpoints (`entire/checkpoints/v1`
branch and `refs/entire/checkpoints/*`, read via `git cat-file`). Deletion
originates in the capture layer: `entire checkpoint delete` removes a checkpoint
from the v1 branch tip, locally and on checkpoint remotes. The brain's job is to
mirror git: when a checkpoint is gone from the refs, the brain drops everything
derived from it at the next refresh.

The brain-local privacy layer (session tombstones + exclude/include/purge +
read gates) was an explicit stopgap "until a capture-layer exclusion contract
exists" (commit `4b5cdfd3`, 2026-08-07). That contract direction is now chosen.
PR #586 already retired the instant-suppression guarantee: retrieval emission no
longer takes any lock; a policy change takes effect on the next command. This
task removes the rest of the layer.

Approved rules:
- Facts: on rebuild, drop provenance entries citing sessions whose checkpoints
  are gone; drop a distilled fact only when it has no provenance left. Authored
  facts (`remember`, no session anchor) are never touched.
- Hosted retraction of already-synced facts is OUT OF SCOPE: the nightly job
  handles it.
- Deletion converges at the next refresh (the watch daemon ticks anyway).
  "Stop serving now" = `entire checkpoint delete … && entire brain refresh`.
  Document this; do not rebuild any per-response enforcement.

## What to delete

1. Tombstone store and flows: `internal/cli/internal/brainstore/tombstones.go`,
   `read_guard.go` consumers, `session_privacy.go` / `session_privacy_verify.go`
   (exclude/include/purge executors, privacy transactions, rollback machinery),
   the `privacy` command family (list/exclude/include/purge).
2. Read gates: `requirePrivacyDerivedRead`, `privacyDerivedReadGate`,
   `internal/cli/patterns/derived_gate.go` (DerivedReadGate / RequireDerivedRead),
   `revalidateRetrievalResponsePrivacy`, and the per-response policy machinery:
   `CaptureRetrievalPrivacyPolicy`, `ValidateRetrievalPrivacyPolicies`,
   `WithLockedRetrievalPrivacyPolicies`, `RetrievalPrivacyPolicy`,
   `commitRetrievalResponse`'s validation, the race seams
   (`beforeRetrievalResponsePrivacyRecheck`,
   `beforeRetrievalResponsePrivacyEmissionCheck`).
3. The locked mutation wrappers that exist only for policy linearization:
   `runPrivacyLinearizedPatternMutation` (5 call sites: recall_evidence is
   already off it; patterns verify self-locks via
   `patterncore.WithCorpusMutationLocked`; check each remaining site for what
   mutual exclusion its body actually needs and give it a direct lock), and the
   member-policy locks in `BuildWorkspaceCorpus`
   (`internal/cli/patterns/workspace_corpus.go:91`). Note the comment at
   `workspace_patterns.go:745`: workspace verify and skill synthesis use those
   locks as mutual exclusion against each other — replace with an explicit
   workspace-brain lock, not silence.
4. Tombstone-aware ingestion: `partitionTombstonedSessions` in export, the
   history/conversation index skip of excluded sessions, doctor's privacy
   states, viz guard plumbing (`Server.Guard`, `requestSessionGuard`,
   `privacyResponseMiddleware` policy capture — the middleware can likely go
   entirely; response buffering too, unless kept for write-error atomicity).
5. Output buffering (`bufferRetrievalCommandOutput`) exists only for the
   privacy boundary. Optional: keep the buffering (it also prevents partial
   output on render errors) but strip the policy parameter. Judgment call;
   do not keep dead parameters.

## What to add

1. Strict-mirror sweep: refresh drops every brain artifact not reachable from
   current checkpoint refs. Remove the deliberate retain-last-copy behavior in
   `internal/cli/export.go` (~lines 403-419: unavailable sessions' cached
   transcripts are kept as "the only surviving copy" — that contradicts the
   mirror model).
2. Provenance-based fact drop in refresh/rebuild, per the approved rule above.
   Facts carry `provenance[].session_id`; sessions present = sessions in the
   current checkpoint catalog.
3. A replacement for the privacy canary test: plant a secret in one session of
   a test repo's checkpoint branch, delete that checkpoint from the v1 tip,
   run refresh, assert the secret is absent from the sessions tree, history
   index, FTS, conversation store, and facts, while other sessions survive.
   The old canary (purge-based) goes with the purge command.

## Known coordination points

- `entire checkpoint delete` is per-checkpoint and leaves sibling checkpoints
  of the same session; a session-level delete and a merge-surviving deletion
  record (anti-resurrection across clones) belong to the entire CLI repo, not
  this task. The brain-side mirror is correct regardless: it reflects whatever
  the refs say.
- The branch-pruning work (merged/deleted branches' memory stores) runs in the
  tegucigalpa workspace in parallel; overlap is limited to export.go and the
  facts manifest. Coordinate before touching `updateFactSourceManifestLocked`.

## Validation

- Replacement canary above is the core proof.
- Expect large test deletions: everything asserting PrivacyDirtyCode flows,
  late-tombstone rejection, privacy commands, derived gates. Deleting a test is
  correct when the guarantee is retired; replacing it is required when the
  guarantee moved (canary).
- `gofmt -l -s` and `go vet` clean (CI gate; no oxfmt binary in this repo).
- Run `go test` directly on touched packages; `mise run check` fails locally
  for a missing gotestsum. The cli suite runs near the 600 s timeout.

## Evidence and history

- Brain memories (branch `main` unless noted): `fact:1d10ce176f39425716a28b6e`
  (four-cause customer diagnosis, branch `evisdren/brain_locked-write.lock-fix`),
  `fact:6a5a0feef41ccfa33e37a291` (emission-lock fix decision),
  `fact:991cb0f38f554cd002f17967` (tombstone gate on read path — superseded by
  this work), `fact:4822420d42c08bb73645bdcd` (repo-wide write lock rationale).
- PR #586 (emission lock removal), commit `4b5cdfd3` (privacy layer
  introduction, states the stopgap intent in its message).
- Retrieve more with:
  `entire brain recall "<question>" --branch main --json`

Branch created, brief and recall done. Two recalled constraints materially shape the design:

1. **Branch stores are not single-branch-pure**: hosted pull deliberately rebuilds a branch store from the repo-wide fact feed, so a store can hold records stamped for other branches. Prune logic must not assume purity.
2. A prior rejection on record: orphan-sweep-style deletion without explicit branch retirement was rejected in another subsystem — deletion needs explicit tracking, not inference.

**Proposed design for sign-off — `memories prune`:**

- New subcommand beside `gc`: `entire brain memories prune` (gc prunes facts *within* a branch; prune removes *whole dead branch stores* — different units, separate verbs).
- **Eligible**: a branch store whose branch no longer exists as `refs/heads/<b>` or `refs/remotes/origin/<b>` — the inverse of the existing `factsBranchIsReal` check (`facts_admin_cmd.go:387`). Never the default branch, never the current branch.

- **Deliberately not automatic.** A deleted remote branch with never-promoted memories would be silently destroyed by a refresh-time sweep; durable memories deserve an explicit, listed, forced deletion. Instead, `status`/`brief` get a one-line warning when prunable stores exist, pointing at the command. (The stateless arc can revisit automation once facts derive from checkpoints.)

- **Branch keying already lost this argument once.** v1/v2 sync used branch-keyed heads and was rejected for v3 because facts synced under `foo` never reached `main` — the per-fact wire that replaced it is repo-wide. The local store just never caught up with that decision.
- The recorded "0 results on your branch, 152 other branches hold memories" gotcha — which your own brief prints every session in this repo — is the UX cost of the same design.

**The past-versions problem**, concretely — three cases, two already have machinery:

Old binaries already refuse a newer schema with an upgrade message, and there's a recorded decision that writers must refuse rather than round-trip unknown layouts. input.content:
# Plan: one flat per-repo memory store (remove branch keying)

## Decisions (made by Evis, 2026-11-02 — do not re-litigate)

1. Retrieval is flat: every branch sees all memories. No branch scoping.
2. `memories promote` is deleted outright. Sync is the only command that moves
   memories. The proposal framework (review queue, keep-both conflicts) is
   deleted too.
3. Migration order is build → verify → delete: construct the flat store, merge
   and dedupe every branch store into it, verify the result is durably written
   and complete, and only then delete the branch files.
4. `--branch` on recall/brief/gc becomes a metadata filter over the record's
   branch field; it no longer selects a store.
5. Upgrade promise: a user on 0.2.x, 0.3.x, or 0.4.x upgrades and their
   memories move into the per-repo store automatically.

## Why (recorded evidence)

- Hosted is already repo-wide: v1/v2 branch-keyed sync heads were rejected for
  v3 (facts synced under `foo` never reached `main`); the frozen per-fact wire
  carries a repo-wide set.
- Hosted pull already dumps the repo-wide feed into the current branch's store
  (recorded gotcha, COR-2126) — local branch keying already duplicates the same
  set per branch. Customer evidence: 540 branch folders, 343k facts, mostly
  copies of main's ~1k, 13.5M proposal lines from per-prompt keep-both promote.
- Recorded gotcha: recall/brief return 0 facts on a fresh branch while 150+
  other branches hold memories.

## Current state (verified in source, 2026-11-02)

The repository store half-exists. `factstore.Load/Write`
(internal/cli/internal/factstore/factstore.go:107,220) already route through
`facts/store.json` (`repoFactStore`: a records map keyed by fact ID plus
per-branch Views of {id, override} entries). The compat adapter
(repo_fact_compat.go) reconciles legacy branch NDJSON files written by old
clients back into the store, and Write republishes legacy projections.
Payloads still live in the legacy files (store schema 2 is a near-bodyless
marker) so old clients can purge them — a constraint the privacy-layer
removal (separate workspace) eliminates.

## Target

- `facts/store.json` (repo store schema 3): flat records map WITH payloads.
  No Views. `branch` stays as a record field (metadata only).
- No `facts/<branch>/facts.ndjson` files, no proposals files, no vitality
  per-branch logs (consolidate to one log).
- Deleted: promote command, review command, factmerge.Proposal +
  ApplyProposal/RejectProposal/dedupeProposals/conflictComponents, keep-both
  machinery, loadFactProposals/writeFactProposals, countFactProposals,
  LoadAllBranches, MissingBranchStores/UnreadableBranchStores (manifest no
  longer declares branches), promote/review tests.
- Manifest facts source: drop Branches and Proposals fields; totals come from
  the one store. `updateFactSourceManifestLocked` becomes O(store).
- Distill reconcile: conflicts that queued proposals now keep both facts with
  no queue (sync settlement already handles cross-machine supersedes). Verify
  against reconcile.go / reconcile_batch.go / cor-2184 staged-candidate
  invariant during implementation.
- Sync: pull writes the feed into the flat store directly (no per-branch
  rebuild); push reads the flat store. The wire itself is frozen — do not
  touch it. Verify what `synced_branches` bookkeeping means and collapse it.

## Migration (new binary, first refresh or fact mutation, under write lock +
distill-pass lock)

1. Reuse `reconcileRepoFactStore`: it already folds schema-1 snapshots,
   legacy branch files, and digest checkpoints, with retirement-wins rules.
2. Flatten: union every view's records by content-derived ID via
   factmerge.Upsert (provenance union; the COR-2220 repair established this
   folding is lossless). Generate zero proposals.
3. Write the flat store atomically; re-read and verify: every record ID from
   every source file is present in the store (set equality), counts logged.
4. Only after verification: move legacy branch dirs to
   `facts/.legacy-<timestamp>/` (rename, not delete) and drop Views. A later
   release GCs the renamed dirs. Pending proposals files are dropped (the
   framework they feed is gone); count them in the migration summary line.
5. Bump the brain manifest SchemaVersion 4 -> 5 and the repo store schema
   2 -> 3.

Idempotent: a migrated brain has no legacy dirs and a v3 store; re-running is
a no-op.

## Old-version behavior after migration (the one-way door)

- v0.4 binaries fail closed on forward-version store ("corrupt or
  forward-version stores fail closed" — Load's documented contract). VERIFY
  during implementation that this is true for the manifest too:
  manifest/read.go:96 gates only `version < MinSchemaVersion`; confirm there
  is an upper gate (supported_schema_version handling) so a v5 manifest makes
  old binaries refuse loudly instead of half-reading. If there is no upper
  gate in released binaries, the fallback is layout-level: they see empty
  branch stores (quiet memory loss) — in that case add a sentinel legacy file
  whose content old parsers reject with a clear message, if their error
  surfaces permit. This is the single riskiest compat item in the plan.
- v0.2/0.3 binaries predate store.json: they see empty branch files and may
  write new ones that nothing reads. Accepted: upgrade is one-way; the next
  new-binary run reports orphan legacy files rather than silently merging
  them (reconcile is removed with the compat adapter).

## Staging (two PRs)

- PR 1 (deletion-first, independent of layout): delete promote + the proposal
  framework + review command. Shrinks the surface PR 2 must move.
- PR 2: flat store with payloads + migration + schema bumps + flip every
  reader/writer + delete branch machinery + sync pull/push simplification +
  `--branch` metadata filtering + consolidate vitality logs.

## Validation

- Migration test matrix: a fixture brain per source layout (schema-1
  snapshot, v0.3-style branch files, v0.4 store+views, mixed), each asserting
  set-equality of record IDs before/after, provenance union on duplicates,
  retirement never revived, legacy dirs renamed only after verify.
- Flat retrieval: recall/brief on a fresh branch return facts recorded on
  other branches; `--branch` filters by metadata.
- The customer-shaped fixture: many branches each holding a copy of the same
  facts -> one store with one copy and unioned provenance.
- gofmt -l -s + go vet (CI gate); `go test` directly on touched packages
  (no gotestsum locally; cli suite near the 600s timeout).

## Coordination

- Privacy-layer removal workspace (handoff-privacy-layer-removal.md): both
  touch export.go and the facts manifest; purge-compat ("payloads live in
  files clients can purge") is the stated reason payloads still live in
  legacy files — these two efforts together remove that constraint. The
  single-store PR 2 should land before the privacy workspace rewrites fact
  filtering, or rebase costs double.
- Hosted retraction of dropped/duplicated facts: nightly job (decided).

content.text:
**Bugbot's finding was real, and it's fixed and pushed (`8c8fadc0`).**

The bug: my keep-both rewrite cross-linked a conflict pair *at apply time*, but a ruling's target can be a cluster member that publishes in a **later wave** — it was legitimately in the agent's EXISTING list as comparison context. At apply time the target wasn't in the result set yet, so the pair silently published unlinked, invisible to the nightly compaction loop that's supposed to settle it.

The fix: collect `(candidate, target)` pairs during apply and cross-link them once after every ruling has landed — order-independent. A pair whose target never landed (hallucinated id) stays unlinked, since the ruling is advisory and the candidate is already published.

The regression test was its own small adventure: it drives a 51-member cluster into two waves, and my first two versions failed on wrong assumptions — cluster member order isn't chronological, and (the interesting one) wave 2's EXISTING list gets capped to the **50 most recently updated** facts, so the older stored fact drops out of the prompt entirely. The final test derives expected pairs from the agent's actual prompt input instead of assuming them, which also documents that cap behavior.

**Finding resolved on trail 2718.** The trail review flagged a real one-time behavior change: with the `pending` guard gone, legacy candidates that an old queued proposal held back will publish on the first distill after upgrading.

I addressed it as a **documented deliberate transition, not a code guard**, because both alternatives are worse:
- *Skipping* legacy candidates strands facts that only the now-deleted `memories review` could ever publish — invisible forever.
- *Replaying* the stale queue applies old adjudications against a store that has moved on.

Re-adjudication through the new keep-both path gives each legacy candidate a fresh ruling and cross-links, at a bounded one-time agent cost — and the nightly compaction loop settles whatever coexists.

- Comment at the exact flagged line (`reconcile_batch.go:49`) stating the choice and why — pushed as `7e59ac50`.
- PR #587 body gained a "One-time behavior change on upgrade" section.

**Fixed and pushed (`1462861c`), bugbot thread answered.**

Bugbot's second finding was correct and worth taking seriously: my earlier "derive expectations from the prompt" refactor had quietly made the regression test vacuous. EXISTING is ranked newest-first (`activeFactsAtPaths`, reconcile.go:224), so the scripted `merge 2` was targeting the stored fact — already applied — and the test would have passed even with the cross-link bug present.

The fix:
- The test runner now **locates the wave-2 member explicitly** — the one cluster member absent from wave 1's CANDIDATES but present in its EXISTING list — and rules against that number, immune to ranking order.
- **A/B verified**: I temporarily reverted the production fix to the old link-at-apply code → test fails; restored the post-pass linking → test passes. The pin now provably bites.

The production fix itself was never wrong — only its test coverage was. #587 is back to CI on the new commit; the trail finding from earlier remains resolved.

- `MigrateRepository(brainDir string) (MigrationSummary, error)` — standing idempotent reconcile: fold → write → **verify** (re-read, every folded id present; failure leaves legacy dirs untouched) → park dirs to `facts/.legacy-<unixts>/<dir>/` (rename, never delete; damaged/unfoldable lines survive there). Bugbot found a real high-severity regression in your distill flip (PR #590, distill_cmd.go:1122-1143 + 1266-1272): a SCOPED --force run (--branch X, or --max-sessions N deferring sessions) pre-drops ALL active distilled facts repo-wide in ensureStore but only re-derives its scope — everything outside the scope is silently lost until some later run re-derives it. The old per-branch ensureBranch dropped only the visited branch, and lazy loading protected deferred branches; the flat store lost that granularity. --session+--force is already refused; --branch/--max-sessions are not, and refusing them is not acceptable (capped force is the supported backfill flow you built at line 1324).

Fix with a post-run scoped sweep replacing the pre-drop. Decided semantics:
1. Remove the force pre-drop from ensureStore entirely.
2. Track this run's rebuiltSessions (session ids fully distilled this run — under force that is every session actually visited, not deferred, not filtered out) and regeneratedFactIDs (every fact id upserted by this run's extraction/reconcile).
3. On the FINAL flush only, under force, after rebaseFactsOntoDisk: drop a record iff Origin==distilled AND Status==active AND !regeneratedFactIDs[id] AND it has at least one provenance session id AND every provenance session id is in rebuiltSessions. Authored, retired/superseded, zero-session-provenance, and any fact citing an unrebuilt session are all kept.
4. Consequence to encode in tests and comments: a full unscoped --force no longer drops facts whose source sessions left the checkpoint catalog — that is now the mirror sweep's job (facts_mirror provenance drop), not force's. Update TestForceRebuildDropsDistilledFactsRepoWideButKeepsAuthored accordingly.
5. Re-derive the force cache semantics in flushFactStoresLocked: the "newCache only, mid-run" rule existed because the pre-drop made prevCache fingerprints dangerous after an interruption. With no pre-drop, re-reason from the invariant: an interrupted force run must lose no facts from sessions it never reached, and a rerun must still re-distill whatever the interrupted run did not finish; the final-flush sweep must never run on a non-final flush. Simplify if the old complexity is now unneeded; keep whatever is still load-bearing, with the comment updated to the real reason.
6. Check rebaseFactsOntoDisk's force parameter and the force no-op detection around distill_cmd.go:2895 against the new model; adjust if they assumed the pre-drop.
7. Keep the --session+--force refusal and the line-1324 deferred-cache-drop behavior.
8. New regression tests: (a) force + --max-sessions=1 over two sessions → the deferred session's facts survive the final flush, and the deferred session re-derives on the next run; (b) force full scope → a stale fact (provenance fully within rebuilt sessions, not regenerated) is dropped while authored/retired/out-of-scope survive; (c) force + --branch drops stale facts only from that branch's sessions.
9. Gates: gofmt -l -s, go vet ./internal/cli/, go test -count=1 ./internal/cli/ -run 'Distill|Force|Reconcile' first, then the full ./internal/cli/ suite once. Do not commit; report what changed and the gate results.

input.message:
Four more findings on PR #590 / trail change 481 — two bugbot (distill force sweep follow-ups to your fix) and two trail-review (hosted sync flat-store interactions). Fix all four with regression tests. Do not commit.

1. BUGBOT medium, distill_cmd.go:2949-2959 + 1179-1182 + 2899-2912 — "Force sweep drops concurrent distilled facts". A distilled+active fact committed to disk by ANOTHER writer during the run (sync settlement, another process) is adopted by rebaseFactsOntoDisk and then deleted by the final force sweep when its cited sessions happen to be in this run's rebuilt set (the old `existed` guard died with the pre-drop). Fix: rebase already diffs baseline vs disk — collect the ids it adopts or updates from disk (present-on-disk-but-not-in-baseline, or changed-on-disk) and exempt them from the sweep exactly like regeneratedFactIDs. Invariant: the force sweep may only delete records that were in this run's own baseline.

2. BUGBOT medium, distill_cmd.go:1244-1276 — "Resume leftovers survive a force rebuild". Resume reconciliation publishes leftover candidates before extraction and records them in regeneratedFactIDs, so the sweep protects them even when this force run re-derives their sessions and does not re-produce them. Fix: under --force, resume-phase publications are NOT regenerated-protected — the sweep's provenance rule governs them (leftovers from rebuilt sessions sweep if stale; leftovers citing out-of-scope sessions survive via the provenance rule). Think through the merge-target edge: a resume merge ruling that mutates an existing target absorbs the leftover's provenance — decide what keeps a completed force pass from deleting a target that only resume touched, and encode the decision in a comment + test. Invariant: an interrupted force pass's leftovers must not outlive a completed force pass that fully rebuilt their sessions, and must survive when their sessions were out of scope.

3. TRAIL medium (hosted_sync.go:456) — pull eviction was written for per-branch stores: it evicts existing records that lack local provenance and whose anchors are unreachable from the CURRENT branch HEAD. In the flat store that deletes teammate facts pulled while on another branch every time you sync elsewhere. Fix: apply the reachability filter to INCOMING feed records only; never evict an already-stored record merely because the current branch's ancestry cannot reach its anchors. Decide (and document) what DOES evict a stored teammate fact now — hosted retraction/settlement remains; if anchor-gone-from-the-whole-repo eviction is still wanted, it belongs to the mirror sweep, not per-branch reachability. Invariant: a teammate fact pulled on any branch stays recallable until hosted retracts it or the mirror sweep drops it.

4. TRAIL medium (facts_hosted_binding.go:50) — readHostedFactsBinding returns the first sorted legacy per-branch hosted-target.json and ignores the rest. When legacy markers disagree (branches bound to different hosted repos/APIs), the flat store silently syncs everything to whichever sorts first. Fix: read all legacy markers; if they agree on the target identity, adopt it (and write the flat binding); if they disagree, return an error telling the user to re-run `memories sync` to choose the target — never pick silently.

Gates: gofmt -l -s, go vet ./internal/cli/, scoped tests (Distill|Force|Hosted|Sync|Binding), full ./internal/cli/ once, and scripts/test-memory-storage-compat.sh (items 3/4 touch the sync paths the released scenarios exercise). Report what changed per finding and the gate results.
